children: By Kate King
Manhattan's Fifth Avenue reclaimed its spot as the corridor with the world's highest retail-rent prices, the latest prize in the city's accelerating real-estate recovery.
Rents on Fifth Avenue have jumped an average 35% over the past year, far outpacing 3% growth worldwide, according to real-estate-services firm Cushman & Wakefield.

Tenants paid an average of $2,700 a square foot to lease space on the upper portion of New York's famed shopping strip over the past year. At that price, a retailer is spending more than $1 million in annual rent for any space larger than 371 square feet, about the size of a two-car garage. And flagship retail stores are far larger than that.
Retail rents on Fifth Avenue beat out those on London's New Bond Street, which held the title last year, and Milan's Via Montenapoleone which also previously topped the list.

Fifth Avenue's return to the top for the first time since 2023 shows that fashion houses and other retailers are once again competing to plant their flags on the most exclusive strip of the avenue — spanning about half a mile from the Saks Fifth Avenue department store at 49th Street to the southeastern corner of Central Park on 60th Street.

The shopping corridor boasts names such as jeweler Tiffany, luxury department store Bergdorf Goodman and a 24-hour Apple store. The strip attracts a wide range of shoppers and tourists, giving brands valuable exposure.
"Fifth Avenue in New York as a whole continues to be of the utmost importance for brands," said Mike O'Neill of Cushman & Wakefield.

New York's other real-estate sectors are similarly outperforming this year, especially among top-tier properties. Office vacancy continues to fall in Manhattan, and asking rents for high-end buildings hit a record-high $87 a square foot in the third quarter, according to Cushman & Wakefield.

Hotel owners in the city, meanwhile, have been able to hike average room rates 7% so far this year, to $328 a night, according to data firm CoStar, outpacing room-rate growth both nationwide and among the U.S.'s top 25 markets.

Fifth Avenue's revitalization marks a significant turnaround from not only the depths of the pandemic but also a contraction that plagued the corridor in the years prior, dragging rents down to as low as $1,500 a square foot in 2019 as retailers closed stores because of high costs and the rise of e-commerce.

Momentum began to build in late 2023, when the fashion house Prada paid more than $800 million to buy the building that houses its store on Fifth Avenue as well as the building next door. Luxury conglomerate Kering bought its own property soon after for nearly $1 billion.
The availability rate on upper Fifth Avenue dropped 4.4 percentage points over the last year, to 13% in the third quarter.

Tech giant Meta Platforms inked a 10-year lease for its Meta Lab flagship next to luxury jeweler Harry Winston. Opened to showcase its artificial-intelligence glasses, the first level of Meta Lab feels like a Warby Parker crossed with an Apple store. Customers can try out the company's virtual-reality headsets in the back.

The upstairs floor reflects retail's increasing focus on integrating experiences with shopping. DJs play sets from a large circular booth on Sunday afternoons. A small cafe serves complimentary coffee while guests wait for their glasses to be customized.

The lower portion of Fifth Avenue, between Bryant Park and 49th Street, has also benefited from surging retailer demand. Souvenir shops and low-priced and other retailers have been replaced over the years with outerwear brands like Arc'teryx and North Face, trendy Gen Z shops like Edikted and athleisure retailers such as On.

"There's very few remaining artifacts of the schlocky cheap retail as you get down toward Bryant Park," said Josh Rabina, whose family firm has developed and owned New York City real estate for three generations.

Rabina recently signed a lease with Utah-based lifestyle outerwear brand Kühl to fill the retail portion of his new supertall skyscraper at 520 Fifth Avenue. Kühl Chief Executive Nate Fay said its surveys consistently found that customers wanted a store in New York. The company searched for a location for two years before landing in the 3,000-square-foot spot.

The holiday season is a peak period on Fifth Avenue, with daily pedestrian volume swelling to 1.5 million during the month of December. Retailers are already starting to festoon their storefronts with garland and colored lights.
On a recent afternoon, workers were busy building the holiday window displays at Bergdorf Goodman as Elicia Starkman exited the department store with a shopping bag on her arm.
"I was on a quest to find a pair of boots, and I found them," said Starkman, who was in town from Los Angeles.
